h1: New York to Washington state car shipping
heroSub: The longest lane we run in the lower 48: about 2,850 miles along I-90 from New York to Seattle, eight to ten days on the truck, and a few things about Puget Sound delivery worth knowing before you book.
intro:
This page is about New York to Washington state car shipping: Seattle, Tacoma, the Eastside, Spokane, and the rest of the Evergreen State, not Washington, DC. The run from the NYC metro to Seattle is roughly 2,850 miles and takes eight to ten days on an open carrier, with a running mid-size sedan typically pricing at $1,400 to $1,550. It is the longest domestic lane we book.

If you did mean the capital, we ship there too: New York to Washington, DC is about 230 miles, usually one day on the truck, and $400 to $500 for a sedan. It rides with our Carolina-bound loads down I-95, and the DC row sits at the bottom of the table below. Use the quote tool beside the headline for either destination.

sections.h2: I-90 end to end: the road from New York to Seattle
sections.html:
Interstate 90 is the longest interstate in the country, and on this lane the car rides nearly all of it. From the city the truck heads up the Thruway to Albany, west through Buffalo to Cleveland and Chicago, up to Minneapolis, then the long empty stretch across South Dakota and Montana past Billings and Missoula, over the Idaho panhandle to Spokane, and over Snoqualmie Pass into Puget Sound. Carriers run it in about seven driving days at 400 to 450 miles a day, with the pickup and delivery stops stretching it to eight to ten.

Because the whole lane runs through upstate, pickups from our Albany, Schenectady, and Buffalo offices sit directly on the route. A Buffalo pickup is about 450 miles shorter than a Long Island pickup and prices roughly $100 lower.

sections.h2: Winter on Snoqualmie Pass and across Montana
sections.html:
From November through March, two pieces of I-90 slow this lane down. The Montana stretch between Billings and Missoula crosses Bozeman Pass and Lookout Pass, and the state closes it to trucks in whiteouts. Then Snoqualmie Pass, 50 miles east of Seattle, gets some of the heaviest snow of any interstate pass; WSDOT requires chains on commercial trucks during storms and closes the pass several times a winter for avalanche control.

Budget an extra day or two for a December through February delivery. The cars themselves are fine on the deck; it is the schedule that moves. Summer brings the fastest transits of the year, though June through August demand lifts the price by about $100.

sections.h2: Seattle, the Eastside, Tacoma, and the Sound: where the truck can go
sections.html:
Seattle is a hard city for a 75-foot car hauler. Capitol Hill, Queen Anne, and Phinney Ridge have steep grades the truck cannot stop on; Ballard, Wallingford, and Fremont are craftsman neighborhoods with narrow streets, parked cars on both sides, and mature trees. Rain is a non-issue, but mossy, sloped driveways are a problem for unloading, so plan a handoff on a flat arterial like Aurora Avenue or 15th Avenue NW, or in a big-box lot. The Eastside is easier: Bellevue, Redmond, and Kirkland have wide suburban streets and corporate campus lots. Tacoma, Everett, and Olympia sit right on I-5 and are straightforward drops.

Anything that requires a ferry costs more. Bainbridge, Whidbey, Vashon, the Kitsap Peninsula, and the Olympic Peninsula all add a ferry fare, a day, and typically $150 to $300, because the carrier either rides the boat or hands off to a small truck. Learn how meeting points work on our door-to-door car shipping page.

sections.h2: Spokane and Eastern Washington as the cheaper drop
sections.html: Spokane is 280 miles east of Seattle, on I-90 before the mountains, and it prices $100 to $150 lower than Seattle because the carrier never crosses Snoqualmie. The Tri-Cities (Richland, Kennewick, Pasco), Yakima, and Wenatchee are also reachable without the pass via I-82 or US-97, and sit between the Spokane and Seattle prices. If you are willing to drive the last leg yourself, an Eastern Washington drop is the cheapest way to get a car into the state. Portland, Oregon works the same way for southwest Washington: Vancouver, WA is a Portland delivery for pricing purposes, and a Portland drop runs about $50 under Seattle because carriers can continue down I-5 to California with the rest of the load.

sections.h2: Who ships this lane: Amazon, Microsoft, Boeing, UW, and the Navy
sections.html:
Most of our Seattle traffic is corporate relocation. New hires and transfers to Amazon in South Lake Union, Microsoft in Redmond, and Boeing in Everett and Renton run year-round, and many employers reimburse car shipping, so keep the bill of lading and invoice. University of Washington students move in late September and out in June, with a Husky Stadium lot as the usual campus handoff. The military side is substantial too: Joint Base Lewis-McChord south of Tacoma, Naval Base Kitsap at Bremerton and Bangor, Naval Station Everett, and NAS Whidbey Island. Bremerton and Whidbey are ferry destinations, which is why military car shipping customers often choose a Tacoma or Everett handoff instead.

Washington is one of the most EV-heavy markets in the country, and EVs ship fine on open carriers at 30 to 60 percent charge; heavy models like a Rivian can carry a $100 to $200 weight surcharge.

sections.h2: The no-sales-tax myth and Washington registration
sections.html: A common idea is that shipping a car in from a lower-tax state saves money in Washington. It does not. Washington charges use tax on a vehicle brought into the state by a new resident, based on its value, when you title it, with a credit for sales tax already paid to another state. New York sales tax usually covers it for a car you have owned, but a recently purchased vehicle can owe the difference. Check the Washington Department of Licensing before you count on any savings. New residents have 30 days after establishing residency to get Washington plates, and Washington has no emissions testing since 2020, so the DOL visit is title, odometer, and a VIN inspection if the car is out of state. Run the car shipping checklist so the title and photos are ready for pickup.

faqs.q: How long does it take to ship a car from New York to Seattle?
faqs.a: Plan on eight to ten days on the truck after pickup, plus a pickup window of one to five days once you book. Drivers cover about 400 to 450 miles a day on I-90 with stops. Between November and March, closures on Snoqualmie Pass or the Montana passes can add a day or two, so leave slack in winter travel plans.

faqs.q: What does New York to Washington state car shipping cost?
faqs.a: A running mid-size sedan on an open carrier from the NYC metro to the Seattle area typically costs $1,400 to $1,550. Spokane runs $100 to $150 less, ferry destinations $150 to $300 more. SUVs and pickups add $100 to $250, enclosed transport adds 30 to 50 percent, and a Buffalo or Albany pickup saves about $100.

faqs.q: Do you ship to Washington, DC too?
faqs.a: Yes. New York to Washington, DC is about 230 miles down I-95, usually one day on the truck, and $400 to $500 for a sedan on an open carrier. It runs almost daily out of our Bronx and Long Island offices. This page covers Washington state; the DC row in the table is there so the two are not confused.

faqs.q: Can the carrier deliver to my house on Capitol Hill or in Ballard?
faqs.a: Usually not to the door. Seattle's steep hills and narrow craftsman streets keep full-size haulers on the arterials, so the driver will call ahead and meet you on a flat main road or in a large lot nearby. If you need delivery into a tight street or a sloped driveway, a smaller truck can sometimes be arranged for an added fee.

faqs.q: Will I avoid sales tax by shipping a car into Washington?
faqs.a: No. Washington charges use tax when a new resident titles a vehicle, with a credit for sales tax paid to another state. A car you have owned and paid New York tax on usually owes little or nothing; a recent purchase may owe the difference. Confirm the current rules with the Washington Department of Licensing before you rely on any savings.
